examTitle: Signals and Systems Exam (HS 2018, 7 February 2019) - free-text problems

questions.question: The causal continuous-time scalar system $\dot y(t)=a\,y(t)+u(t)$ is discretized using the forward Euler method for a zero-order hold input and a uniformly sampled output, with sampling time $T_s>0$.

parts.question: Determine the values of $T_s$ as a function of $a$ that make the discrete-time system stable.
parts.final_answer: $a>0$: never stable. $a=0$: stable (marginally) for all $T_s$. $a<0$: stable iff $T_s<\frac{2}{|a|}$.
parts.solution: $A_{eu}=1+aT_s$, $B_{eu}=T_s$, so $y[n+1]=(1+aT_s)y[n]+T_su[n]$. Stability requires $|1+aT_s|<1$. If $a>0$ then $1+aT_s>1$: always unstable. If $a=0$ the pole is at 1 and the official key calls this stable for all $T_s$. If $a<0$: $1+aT_s>-1\iff T_s<\frac{2}{|a|}$.

rubric.criterion: a > 0: always unstable (pole 1 + a Ts > 1)
a = 0: stable for every Ts (pole at 1, marginal)
a < 0: condition |1 + a Ts| < 1, i.e. Ts < 2/|a|

parts.question: Determine for which values of $a$ Euler discretization and exact discretization correspond.
parts.solution: Let $M=\begin{bmatrix}a&1\\0&0\end{bmatrix}$. Euler and exact discretization coincide iff $I+T_sM=\sum_{k=0}^\infty\frac{(MT_s)^k}{k!}$, which requires $M^2=\begin{bmatrix}a^2&a\\0&0\end{bmatrix}=0$ (then all higher powers vanish). This holds only for $a=0$.

rubric.criterion: Builds the augmented matrix M = [[a,1],[0,0]]
Equates I + Ts*M with the matrix exponential series, requiring M^2 = 0
Concludes a = 0

questions.question: Consider the discrete-time system $y[n]=a\,y[n-3]+u[n]+0.5\cos(2\pi n)$ with $a\in\mathbb{R}$.

parts.question: Elaborate on linearity, stability, causality, time-invariance and memorylessness as a function of the parameter $a\in\mathbb{R}$. Justify your answer.
parts.final_answer: Non-linear (affine) for all $a$; time-invariant for all $a$; memoryless iff $a=0$; for $|a|<1$ causal and stable; for $|a|>1$ the stable solution is anti-causal.
parts.solution: The term $0.5\cos(2\pi n)$ is an offset (it equals $0.5$ for integer $n$), so the system is affine, not linear (zero input gives non-zero output), for every $a$. The coefficients do not depend on $n$, so the system is time-invariant for every $a$. The output depends only on the current input when $a=0$: memoryless iff $a=0$. For $|a|<1$ the causal recursion is stable (pole $z^3=a$ inside the unit circle). For $|a|>1$ the causal solution is unstable, but the system can be solved backwards in time, which gives a stable anti-causal system. (For $|a|=1$ it is not stable.)

rubric.criterion: Non-linear (affine) for all a, justified (non-zero output for zero input / offset)
Time-invariant for all a, justified
Memoryless iff a = 0
Causal and stable for |a| < 1, justified
Anti-causal and stable for |a| > 1, justified (mentioning the anti-causal case)

parts.accepted_alternatives: Per the official grading remarks, a convincing argument that the system is time-variant (e.g. 'cos is time-variant') is also accepted by the official key, although cos(2*pi*n)=1 for integer n.

questions.question: Consider the cascade of two LTI systems $G_1$ and $G_2$, with impulse responses $h_1[n]=\sin(8n)$ and $h_2[n]=a^ns[n]$, with $|a|<1$ and $s[n]$ the unit step.

parts.question: Determine the output of the system $G_2$ if the input is $u[n]=\delta[n]-a\,\delta[n-1]$, where $\delta[n]$ is the unit impulse.

rubric.criterion: Convolves u with h2 (or uses the z-transform)
Correct algebra: a^n s[n] - a^n s[n-1]
Result delta[n]

parts.question: Determine the output of the cascade of the two systems $G_1$ and $G_2$ if the input is $u[n]=\delta[n]-a\,\delta[n-1]$.
parts.solution: Convolution is associative and commutative, so the order of the systems does not matter: $u*(h_2*h_1)=(u*h_2)*h_1$. By part (a) $u*h_2=\delta[n]$, hence the output is $\delta[n]*\sin(8n)=\sin(8n)$, i.e. the impulse response of $G_1$.

rubric.criterion: Uses commutativity/associativity of convolution (order of cascade does not matter) to apply part (a) first
Correct result y[n] = sin(8n)

questions.question: Consider the signal $x[n]=0$ for $n\le0$, $x[n]=0$ for $n$ odd with $n>0$, and $x[n]=\frac{1}{n^2}$ for $n$ even with $n>0$. Let $X(\Omega)$ be the Fourier transform of $\{x[n]\}$, $Y(\Omega)=e^{j\Omega}X(\Omega)$, $Q(\Omega)=X(\Omega)+Y(\Omega)$, $q[n]$ the inverse Fourier transform of $Q(\Omega)$, and $r[n]=0$ for $n\le0$, $r[n]=0$ for $n$ odd with $n>0$, and $r[n]=q[n]-q[n-2]$ for $n$ even with $n>0$.

parts.question: What is $r[n]$? (Justify that the transforms exist.)
parts.final_answer: $r[n]=0$ for $n\le0$ and for odd $n$; $r[2]=\frac14$; and $r[n]=\frac{1}{n^2}-\frac{1}{(n-2)^2}$ for even $n\ge4$ (e.g. $r[4]=\frac1{16}-\frac14$).
parts.solution: $\sum_{n\ge1}\frac1{n^2}$ converges, so $x$ is absolutely summable and $X(\Omega)$ exists. By linearity $q=x+\mathcal{F}^{-1}(e^{j\Omega}X)$, and $e^{j\Omega}X(\Omega)$ is the transform of $x[n+1]$ (time-shift property), so $q[n]=x[n]+x[n+1]$: $q[0]=0$, $q[1]=q[2]=(\frac12)^2$, $q[3]=q[4]=(\frac14)^2,\ldots$. Then for even $n>0$, $r[n]=q[n]-q[n-2]$: $r[2]=(\frac12)^2-0$, $r[4]=(\frac14)^2-(\frac12)^2$, etc.

rubric.criterion: Argues existence of X(Omega) via absolute summability (sum of 1/n^2 converges)
Uses linearity of the inverse transform
Shows e^{j Omega}X(Omega) corresponds to x[n+1] (time shift), so q[n] = x[n] + x[n+1]
Correct r[n], including r[2]=1/4 and the general even-n formula

parts.accepted_alternatives: Official remark: omitting the n=2 term costs 0.5 points; merely restating q in terms of x earns only 0.5 of the 2 points for the time-shift step.

questions.question: Let $x[n]$ and $y[n]$ be two periodic signals, both with period $N$, with $y[n]\ne0$ for all $n$, and $z[n]=\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}\frac{x[k]}{y[n-k]}$.

parts.question: Is the signal $z[n]$ periodic? If yes, what is its period?

rubric.criterion: States z is periodic, with argument
Period N

parts.question: Let $X[k]$, $W[k]$, $Z[k]$ be the DFS coefficients of $x[n]$, $w[n]=\frac{1}{y[n]}$ and $z[n]$, respectively, with the convention $X[k]=\frac1N\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}x[n]e^{-jk\frac{2\pi}{N}n}$. Express $Z[k]$ as a function of $X[k]$ and $W[k]$.
parts.solution: $Z[k]=\frac1N\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}\sum_{r=0}^{N-1}x[r]w[n-r]e^{-jk\frac{2\pi}{N}n}=\frac1N\sum_{r}x[r]e^{-jk\frac{2\pi}{N}r}\sum_{n}w[n-r]e^{-jk\frac{2\pi}{N}(n-r)}=\frac1N\,(N\,X[k])\,(N\,W[k])=N\,X[k]W[k]$ (using periodicity to shift the inner sum).

rubric.criterion: Writes Z[k] with the double sum (z[n] as circular convolution of x and w)
Splits the exponential e^{-j..n} = e^{-j..(n-r)} e^{-j..r} and swaps the sums, using periodicity
Correct result Z[k] = N X[k] W[k] (the answer X[k]W[k] without the factor N gets 0 for this criterion)

questions.question: A signal $u$ has the form $u[n]=c_0+c_1(-1)^n+c_2\cos(\frac{\pi}{3}n)$ for $n\in\{\ldots,-1,0,1,\ldots\}$, where $c_0,c_1,c_2\in\mathbb{R}$ are fixed but unknown constants. (Hint: $\cos(\frac{\pi}{3})=0.5$.)

parts.question: Design a causal, stable, LTI filter $G$ such that if $u$ has the form above and $y=Gu$, then $y[n]=c_0$ for all $n$. Give the transfer function (or difference equation) and justify causality and stability.
parts.final_answer: $H(z)=\frac{1+z^{-3}}{2}$, i.e. $y[n]=\frac{u[n]+u[n-3]}{2}$ (a causal moving average of order 6 is also valid).
parts.solution: $u[n]=c_0e^{j\Omega_0n}+c_1e^{j\Omega_1n}+\frac{c_2}{2}(e^{j\Omega_2n}+e^{-j\Omega_2n})$ with $\Omega_0=0$, $\Omega_1=\pi$, $\Omega_2=\frac{\pi}{3}$. Need $H(1)=1$, $H(-1)=0$, $H(e^{j\pi/3})=0$, $H(e^{-j\pi/3})=0$. Use an FIR filter (stable) and a delay to make it causal: $H(z)=\alpha(z+1)(z^2-z+1)z^{-3}=\alpha(z^3+1)z^{-3}=\alpha(1+z^{-3})$; $H(1)=1\Rightarrow\alpha=\frac12$. Hence $y[n]=\frac{u[n]+u[n-3]}2$.

rubric.criterion: Rewrites u as complex exponentials with frequencies 0, pi, +-pi/3
Condition H(1) = 1
Condition H(-1) = 0
Condition H(e^{j pi/3}) = 0
Condition H(e^{-j pi/3}) = 0
Argues stability (FIR)
Argues causality (z^-N delay / only past inputs)
Places zeros at -1 and e^{+-j pi/3} (e.g. via (z+1)(z^2 - z + 1))
Normalises gain: alpha = 1/2 so H(1)=1
Gives a correct final causal H(z) / difference equation

parts.accepted_alternatives: Any causal stable filter satisfying the four conditions, including a causal moving average filter of order 6 (the official remarks explicitly accept this and different representations).

questions.question: To identify the coefficients of the transfer function of a causal, stable LTI system $H(z)=\frac{b_0}{1+a_1z^{-1}}$, the signal $u[n]=\frac{e^{j\frac{\pi}{2}n}+e^{-j\frac{\pi}{2}n}}{2}$ is given as input. The DFS coefficients (period $N=4$, convention $x[n]=\frac1N\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}X[k]e^{jk\frac{2\pi}{N}n}$) of the periodic output signal $\{y[n]\}$ are $\{Y[k]\}=\{0,\ 3.2+j1.6,\ 0,\ 3.2-j1.6\}$.

parts.question: Determine the values of the coefficients $a_1$ and $b_0$.
parts.solution: The DFS of the input is $\{U[k]\}=\{0,2,0,2\}$. Hence $H[k]=\frac{Y[k]}{U[k]}$ gives $H(e^{j\pi/2})=H(j)=1.6+0.8j$ (and the conjugate at $k=3$). With $z^{-1}=-j$: $H(j)=\frac{b_0}{1-ja_1}$, so $b_0=(1.6+0.8j)(1-ja_1)=(1.6+0.8a_1)+j(0.8-1.6a_1)$. Imaginary part zero: $a_1=0.5$; real part: $b_0=2$.

rubric.criterion: Correct DFS of the input U = {0, 2, 0, 2}
Computes the frequency response samples H[k] = Y[k]/U[k] = 1.6+0.8j at k=1 (and conjugate at k=3)
Sets up equations for a1, b0 from H(j) = b0/(1 - j a1) (real and imaginary parts, or matrix form)
Correct values a1 = 0.5 and b0 = 2

parts.accepted_alternatives: Official remark: computing everything in the time domain is also possible.

questions.question: Consider the following pairs of signals $\{u_i[n]\}$ and $\{y_i[n]\}$, $i=1,\ldots,4$. Determine whether the signal $\{y_i[n]\}$ can be the output of a discrete-time LTI system given the input $\{u_i[n]\}$. If such a system exists, determine whether the system is unique, i.e. fully defined by this input-output relationship. If such a system does not exist, explain why.

parts.question: $\{u_1[n]\}=\{e^{jn}\}$, $\{y_1[n]\}=\{2e^{jn}\}$.
parts.final_answer: An LTI system exists, but it is not unique.
parts.solution: $e^{jn}$ is an eigenfunction, so an LTI relationship exists if $H(e^{j})=2$. Only this single value of the frequency response is constrained, so the system is not unique.

rubric.criterion: Existence (eigenfunction with H(e^{j1}) = 2)
Not unique (only one frequency response value is specified)

parts.question: $\{u_2[n]\}=\{\cos(n)s[n]\}$, $\{y_2[n]\}=\{2\cos(n)s[n]\}$, where $s[n]$ is the unit step.
parts.final_answer: An LTI system exists and it is unique: $H(\Omega)=2$ (impulse response $2\delta[n]$).
parts.solution: The output is exactly twice the input, so the system with $H(\Omega)=2$ works. Since the input is a non-periodic, causal signal with a broad spectrum, it excites all frequencies and uniquely determines the frequency response $H(\Omega)=2$.

rubric.criterion: Existence (gain 2)
Unique (input has full-band content so H(Omega) = 2 is fully determined)

parts.question: $\{u_3[n]\}$ and $\{y_3[n]\}$ are both periodic and depicted in the time domain in the figure (their common fundamental period is 12).
parts.final_answer: An LTI system exists, but it is not unique.
parts.solution: Both signals are periodic with the same fundamental period ($N=12$), so an LTI relationship exists. However, only the values $H(e^{j\frac{2\pi}{12}k})$ are determined; the remaining values of $H(\Omega)$ can be chosen arbitrarily, so the system is not unique.

rubric.criterion: Existence (same fundamental period)
Not unique (only H at 2*pi*k/12 is constrained)

parts.question: $\{u_4[n]\}$ and $\{y_4[n]\}$ are both periodic and depicted in the time domain in the figure (they have different fundamental periods).
parts.solution: The two signals have different periods. An LTI system cannot create frequency components not present in the input (eigenfunction property), so such a relationship is impossible.

rubric.criterion: States no LTI system exists
Correct reason: different periods / output contains frequencies absent from the input, violating the eigenfunction-eigenvalue property
